label: text
content: ## Multiple sequence alignment (MSA)

label: text
content: So far, we have learned only about pair-wise sequence comparison:

label: text
content: - Global alignment of two sequences

label: text
content: - Local alignment of two sequences

label: text
content: - Mapping of a single read to the reference genome (even if we do this millions of times, we always map only one read at a time!)

label: text
content: But for many applications (especially in the field of evolutionary genetics/genomics) it is usefull to align multiple sequences (>2) to each other at the same time ...

label: text
content: - We want to compare more than two sequences at the same time, that is, we want to align more than two sequences ("multiple sequence alignment", MSA)

label: text
content: - Ideally, the comparison/alignment should be simultaneous; we want to analyze a single alignment containing all sequences, not the list of all possible pairwise alignments

label: text
content: ## From two to many

label: text
content: Sequences may share a common evolutionary history (a common ancestor)

label: text
content: The more similar two sequences, the closer in time is their common ancestor

label: text
content: "Parsimony" for evolutionary changes:

label: text
content: Match: nothing changed during evolution

label: text
content: Mismatch: one of the two sequences changed with respect to the ancestor sequence

label: text
content: - Gap: insertion or a deletion with respect to the ancestor sequence

label: text
content: In this particular example: the final "consensus" (most frequent letters) is exactly (the sound) of the common ancestor word ...

label: text

label: text

label: text
content: $\forall i \in(1\dots k), S_{i}^{\prime}$ is obtained from $S_{i}$ with the insertion of gaps

label: text
content: The alignment $A$ is written with the $S_{i}'$ strings one over the others, in any order: $^{1}$

label: text
content: ## Multiple alignment scores: Sum of Pairs

label: text
content: - The possible ways to align k strings depend on where we place gaps (this actually holds also for k=2)

label: text
content: - Like for k=2, we might choose a formalization where we have a "score" that has to be optimized or a "distance" to be minimized

label: text
content: - As we saw, a multiple alignment implicitly induces a pairwise alignment for every pair $S_{i}, S_{j}$

label: text
content: - We can use the substitution matrix we employed for pairwise alignment, and compute the pairwise alignment score a $( S_{i}, S_{j} )$ for every pair $S_{i}, S_{j}$

label: formula
text
content: - We compute the "Sum of Pairs (SP) score" as the sum of the alignment scores of every possible pair:

label: formula
content:
$$
S P = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k - 1} \sum_ {j = i + 1} ^ {k} a \left(S _ {i}, S _ {j}\right)
$$

label: text
content: - Goal: find the multiple alignment that maximizes this score! This is an optimization (maximization) problem

label: text
content: ## Multiple alignment scores: Sum of Pairs

label: text
content: - The SP-score is essentially a generalization to k strings of the principle we applied to 2 strings

label: text
content: - But it has another fundamental property: like for k=2, the optimal solution can be found by dynamic programming!

label: text
content: - The idea:

label: text
content: For $k = 2$, we use a two-dimensional structure (a matrix)

label: text
content: - For $k = 3$, we use a three-dimensional structure (a cube)

label: text
content: For $k > 3$ , we use a $k$-dimensional structure (a hypercube = hyperlattice)

label: formula
formula
content:
$$
S P = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k - 1} \sum_ {j = i + 1} ^ {k} a \left(S _ {i}, S _ {j}\right)
$$

label: text
content: - But the principle is the same as for k=2: for filling a cell we look at the values in the neighboring cells

label: text
content: - The last cell in the structure (maximum index in each dimension) will then contain the score of the optimal (global) multiple alignment!

label: text
content: - For k=2, we have 3 neighbors

label: text
content: - For k=3, we have 7 neighbors:

label: text
content: - For k, we have $2^{k}-1$ neighbors!

label: text
content: ## Space and time complexity of the approach

label: text
content: We have $k$ strings as input, suppose for sake of simplicity that all strings have the same length $n$, i.e., $|S_{i}| = n \quad \forall i \in (1\dots k)$

label: text
content: - The data structure we fill has $(n + 1)^{k}$ cells $\Rightarrow$ space complexity is $O(n^{k})$

label: text
content: - For filling each cell we compare $2^{k} - 1$ scores $\Rightarrow$ time complexity is $O(2^{k} n^{k})$

label: text
content: - All in all space/time is exponential in the number of strings to be aligned ...

label: text
content: - Important note: $k$ is not a constant here—it is an input value!—therefore ...

label: text
content: ... the multiple sequence alignment problem is NP-hard!

label: text
content: - NP hardness = "non-deterministic polynomial-time" hardness

label: text
content: - It cannot be solved in polynomial time (unless P=NP ...)

label: text
content: In practice, it is considered to be "unfeasible" to align more than 4 sequences with dynamic programming

label: text
content: - Improvements in dynamic programming make it feasible to align up to 6 sequences (but the problem remains NP-hard)

label: text
content: And, it also remains NP-hard if we change the scoring function, for every "reasonable" scoring function which is not trivial

label: text
content: Intuitively, the problem arises from the k in $O(2^{k} n^{k})$

label: text
content: It has been proven to be NP-hard for basically every scoring function employed

label: text
content: ## Dealing with NP-hard problems

label: text
content: (Note: the following is not an exhaustive discussion of NP-hardness and approximate solutions!)

label: text
content: - When we have to face an NP-hard problem, in an "applicative" field (that is, it comes from the formalization of a problem), we have to find a way to solve it anyway; that is, we need to find a way to efficiently align $k>4$ (or $k>6$) sequences

label: text
content: - Different possibilities:

label: text
content: - Change the formalization in order to solve it in polynomial time, hoping that the formalization still captures the "right solution" for the problem

label: text
content: - Explore the space of possible solutions (which is exponential in size), considering only a reasonable polynomial subset of them, hoping that it contains the optimal one

label: text
content: - Design a polynomial time/space algorithm, based on some heuristic, hoping that it will find the optimal solution (or another one very close to it) for most of the "typical" instances that will be provided as input

label: text
content: - Design a polynomial time/space algorithm, based on some heuristic, proving that for every possible input the solution will not be too far (within certain limits) from the optimal one (that is, design an approximation algorithm!)

label: text
content: ## Dealing with NP-hard problems

label: text
content: ## Approximability:

label: text
content: - Suppose that we design a polynomial time algorithm for an NP-hard maximization problem

label: text
content: - For an instance I of the problem, let $A(I)$ be the value/score of the solution found by our algorithm

label: text
content: - Let $M(I)$ the optimal (maximum) value for instance $I$

label: text
content: - If we can prove that there is a constant value $\varepsilon\in(0,1]$ such that for every instance I, we have

label: formula
content:
$$
\frac {A (I)}{M (I)} \geq \varepsilon
$$

label: text
content: then we have designed a "performance guaranteed" approximation algorithm for the problem

label: text
content: Of course we exclude the trivial case $\varepsilon=0$ and want $\varepsilon$ to be as close as possible to 1!

label: text
content: In our case: can we design a polynomial-time algorithm that for each set of k strings to be aligned (each specific set constitutes an instance I) guarantees that the obtained alignment score $A(I)$ is sufficiently close to the maximum $M(I)$ obtained when computing the correpsonding full hypercube?

label: text
content: ## Dealing with NP-hard problems

label: text
content: ## Approximability:

label: text
content: "Approximability" of NP-hard problems has received a lot of attention starting from the late 1990's

label: text
content: Different classes of approximability have been defined for NP-hard problems; these classes tell us how "close" we can get to the optimal solution of the problem, in polynomial time

label: text
content: For some classes, we can prove that "the closer we get" the "more time" (polynomial anyway) we need—that is, we can get as close as we want

label: text
content: - For some classes the bigger is the size of the problem, the farther is our approximate solution

label: text
content: For some classes we cannot even find an approximation algorithm ...

label: text
content: ## Back to multiple sequence alignment

label: text
content: How can we design a polynomial-time algorithm for the multiple sequence alignment problem?

label: text
content: - We know how to compute a pairwise alignment

label: text
content: - We could try to build the multiple alignment as a series of consecutive pairwise alignments

label: text
content: - If we think about the definition, what makes different solutions differ from one another is where we decide to put gaps in the original strings

label: text
content: Thus, if at some step we put the gap in the wrong place, we miss the optimal solution

label: text
content: Heuristic: intuitively, the more similar the input sequences are, the less gaps we have to place during their alignment, the less likely we are to put a gap in the wrong position!

label: text
content: ## The center star algorithm

label: text
content: Input: k strings $S_{1}, S_{2}, \dots S_{k}$

label: text
content: Procedure:

label: text
content: Compute the pairwise alignment of every pair of input strings

label: text
content: Let $a(S_{i}, S_{j})$ be the score of the alignment of strings $S_{i}$ and $S_{j}$

label: text
content: - Let $SP(S_{i}) = \sum_{i \neq j} a(S_{i}, S_{j})$ be the total pairwise alignment score of $S_{i}$ with all other strings

label: text
content: Choose $S_{c}$ to be

label: formula
content:
$$
S _ {c} = \operatorname {a r g m a x} _ {S _ {i}} S P \left(S _ {i}\right)
$$

label: text
content: - This is simply the string with the highest SP, i.e., the string which is globally "more similar" to the other strings of the set

label: text
content: We call this string the "center of the star"

label: text
content: The multiple alignment is built by starting with $S_{c}$ and iteratively, i.e., one by one, adding the other strings as they were aligned to $S_{c}$ in step 1 (i.e., simply using their pairwise alignment with $S_{c}$)!

label: text
content: ## The center star algorithm: example

label: text
content: - We compute all pairwise alignments

label: text
content: - $S_{2}$ is our "center" of the star

label: text
content: E. g., for match=1, mismatch=-1 and gap=-1 we get $SP ( S_{2} )=3$

label: text
content: - The multiple alignment is built by adding all other strings according to their pairwise alignment with $S_{2}$

label: text
content: - The order in which they are added is thus not important

label: text
content: ## The center star algorithm: complexity

label: text
content: Let us for simplicity assume we have k strings of equal length n

label: text
content: Space and time complexity:

label: text
content: - Step 1: pairwise alignment

label: text
content: We produce $k(k-1)/2=O(k^{2})$ pairwise alignments

label: text
content: Each alignment takes $O(n^{2})$ time and space (filling the 2D scoring matrix!)

label: text
content: The overall complexity of the first step is thus $O(k^{2} n^{2})$ time and space, as opposed to $O(n^{k})$ space and $O(2^{k} n^{k})$ time for using a hypercube to perform the optimal multiple sequence alignment ...

label: text
content: In practice, we have additional advantages:

label: text
content: - Actually, if we compute the pairwise alignments sequentially, we only need $O(n^{2})$ space (we can discard the matrix after each pairwise alignment)

label: text
content: - If we perform the $k(k-1)/2$ alignments in parallel, then we only need $O(n^{2})$ wall clock time (but of course more computing power/processor cores)

label: text
content: ## Steps 2 and 3: Choosing the center string and building the final alignment takes $O(nk)$ time

label: text
content: - Hence, the overall time/space complexity is $O \left( k^{2} n^{2} \right)$

label: text
content: ## The center star algorithm: approximation

label: text
content: - With this algorithm, we do not actually compare all the strings to one another

label: text
content: - We just compare all the strings to the center, hoping that the pairwise alignment of each of them would also be found in the optimal multiple alignment

label: text
content: Essentially, we hope that in the optimal alignment the gaps would be placed in the same positions where we place them in the pairwise alignments with the center

label: text
content: How accurate is this approximation?

label: text
content: - We can re-formalize the problem: instead of maximizing the overall similarity (sum of pairs), we can minimize the overall distance (sum of distances)

label: text
content: - If the triangle inequality holds (for the edit distance it does!),

label: formula
content:
$$
z \leq x + y
$$

label: text
content: then we can prove that it is an approximation algorithm with $\varepsilon=2$ . That is, the ratio between the overall distance found by the algorithm and the "minimum" (optimal) overall distance is always equal to or lower than 2!

label: text
content: Thus, in the worst case, the alignment found by the "center star" algorithm has an overall distance between the sequences (the function to be optimized) which is (at worst) twice the optimal overall distance. It can be lower (3/2, 6/5, etc) but never higher (5/2, 7/3, etc)!

label: text
content: Can we produce more "biologically relevant" alignments, regardless of the approximation?

label: text
content: ## Some biological reasoning

label: text
content: - The assumption is that our sequences have a common evolutionary history

label: text
content: - Remember Darwin's "tree of life" for species?

label: text
content: At the sequence level, imagine we can trace the evolutionary history of DNA (or protein) sequences with their "ancestor tree"—in molecular evolution this is called a "phylogenetic tree".

label: text
content: That is, assume we know the true history among different alternatives like these:

label: text
content: - Suppose the evolutionary history is the one shown to the left

label: text
content: - The idea is to keep aligning pairs of sequences, but instead of choosing a "center" string we follow the evolutionary history, going back in time

label: text
content: - That is, we start by aligning the strings that are "closest relatives", then we move back on the tree. In this example:

label: text
content: 1 We align S1 with S2

label: text
content: 2 We align S3 with S4

label: text
content: We somehow "merge" the alignment of (S1,S2) with the alignment of (S3,S4)

label: text
content: ## Some biological reasoning

label: text
content: - The assumption is that our sequences have a common evolutionary history

label: text
content: - Remember Darwin's "tree of life" for species?

label: text
content: At the sequence level, imagine we can trace the evolutionary history of DNA (or protein) sequences with their "ancestor tree"—in molecular evolution this is called a "phylogenetic tree".

label: text
content: That is, assume we know the true history among different alternatives like these:

label: text
content: - Suppose the evolutionary history instead is the one shown to the right

label: text
content: - We again start by aligning the strings that are "closest relatives", then we move back on the tree.

label: text

label: text

label: text

label: text

label: text
content: ## Alignment profile

label: text
content: - One very useful way of describing a multiple alignment is to represent it it as an alignment profile

label: text
content: - For each column of the alignment, the profile represents the frequency with which we find each symbol of the alphabet (including the gap) in that column

label: text
content: Frequencies in each column sum up to 1

label: text
content: x: AC-GCGG-C

label: text
content: y: AC-GC-GAG

label: text
content: z: GCCGC-GAG

label: text
content: - Profiles are a way of representing an MSA in a compact manner

label: text
content: - The drawback is that we lose the information about which sequence each character/symbol belongs to

label: text
content: We know that the profile was built from 3 sequences and that there are two "A" in the first column; but we don't know in which of the 3 sequences these "A"s are ...

label: text
content: ## Weighted dynamic programming

label: text
content: Can we use such this profile to align (add) a fourth sequence?

label: text
content: - We can also use a dynamic programming matrix like for a pairwise global alignment, but we replace one of the two strings by an entire profile

label: text
content: - The rows represent the string to be added

label: text
content: But for the columns we have the profile: not single letters but for each column we have all letters of the alphabet (plus gap) and their respective frequencies in the previous alignment

label: text

label: text
content: ## Weighted dynamic programming

label: text
content: Computing the individual scores for the alignment matrix A:

label: text
content: Given: Profile R with frequencies $R[c,j]$ for character c (including gap) in column j Given: String $X=\left(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\right)$ to be aligned (in the rows of matrix A)

label: text
content: Score of matching character x with column j of the profile:

label: formula
content:
$$
P (x, j) = \sum_ {c \in \Sigma} \sin (x, c) \times R [ c, j ]
$$

label: text
content: $sim(x,c)$ is the cost of aligning x with c (including gaps), $R[c,j]$ is the frequency of char c in column j of the matrix

label: text
content: $A[i,j] = \max \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} A[i - 1,j - 1] + P(x_i,j) & \mathrm{align} x_i \mathrm{to} \mathrm{column} j \\ A[i - 1,j] + \mathrm{gap} & \mathrm{introduce} \mathrm{gap} \mathrm{into} \mathrm{profile} \\ A[i,j - 1] + P("_{-}",j) & \mathrm{introduce} \mathrm{gap} \mathrm{into} x \end{array} \right.$

label: text
content: Here, $sim(x,c)$ will usually be the match score, mismatch penalty or gap penalty, or alternatively the score obtained from a substitution matrix; $sim(-,-) = 0$ for two gaps

$$

$$

label: formula
content:
$$
A [ i, j ] = \max \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} A [ i - 1, j - 1 ] + P \left(x _ {i}, j\right) & \text {a l i g n} x _ {i} \text {t o c o l u m n} j \\ A [ i - 1, j ] + \text {g a p} & \text {i n t r o u c e} g a p \text {i n t o p r o f i l e} \\ A [ i, j - 1 ] + P \left(" ", j\right) & \text {i n t r o u c e} g a p \text {i n t o} x \end{array} \right.
$$

label: text
content:
- Option 1 (diagonal): align $x_{1} = "$ "A" to column $j = 1$ (having $\frac{2}{3}$ "A" and $\frac{1}{3}$ "G")

- $0+P("A",1)=0+\sum_{c\in\Sigma}\operatorname{sim}("A",c)\times R[c,1]=1\times \frac{2}{3}+(-1)\times \frac{1}{3}=\frac{1}{3}$

label: text
content: - Option 2 (from top): gap in profile

label: formula
content:
$$
\triangleright - 1 + (- 1) = - 2
$$

label: text
content: - Option 3 (from left): gap in x

label: formula
content:
$$
- 1 + \sum_ {c \in \Sigma} \sin \left(" -", c\right) \times R [ c, 1 ] = - 1 + (- 1) \times \frac {2}{3} + (- 1) \times \frac {1}{3} = - 2
$$

label: text
content: ## Weighted dynamic programming

label: text
content: - By using the "weighted" version of the update rule, we can fill the matrix as we did in the global alignment of two strings

label: text
content: - At each step, we keep track of the cell that gave the best choice at each step (for backtracing)

label: text
content: - At the end, as usual, cell (n,m) will contain the value of the optimal alignment

label: text
content: - The alignment will be build with a traceback, as in the global alignment of two strings

label: text
content: - Then, according to the resulting alignment, we update the alignment profile by adding the new string we just aligned and recomputing the new frequencies

label: text
content: - We also save the actual alignment as output (final output if all sequences were used; otherwise input to the next step)

label: text
content: - The same principle can be applied to the alignment of two profiles!

label: text
content: - For both rows and columns of the alignment matrix we would have a profiles instead of a string

label: text
content: - The update of the cells can be performed with a "double weighted" version of the rule for global alignment

label: text
content: ## "Progressive" multiple alignments

label: text
content: - Algorithms of this kind are in general said to build a "progressive" multiple alignment

label: text
content: - The key is having the "guide-tree" telling us the order of operations in which the alignment has to be built:

label: text
content: - But, what if we don't have a guide-tree?

label: text
content: Usually we don't! As a matter of fact an MSA is the starting point for inferring the evolutionary history of the sequences, so we will have an evolutionary tree that we could use for guidance only after having performed the multiple alignment ...

label: text
content: - Idea: before proceeding with the alignments, we build the guide tree ourselves, that is, we try to predict the evolutionary history behind the sequences!
